title: Punctual bound suffices for a module bound
statement:
Let $(V,F)$ be a finite-dimensional $\Qlb$-Frobenius module in the
sense of [def-weil-frobenius-module-weights] such that every
eigenvalue $\alpha$ of $F$ satisfies
$|\iota(\alpha)|\leq q^{w/2}$.
Then $(V,F)$ is $\iota$-mixed of weights at most $w$.

proof.text: Induct strongly on the dimension of V. In dimension zero V is subsingleton and has no eigenvalues; it is vacuously pure of weight w. A pure module of weight t <= w is mixed: use the two-term filtration 0 <= V, identify its only quotient with V, and conjugate Frobenius along that identification.

For nonzero V, Mathlib Module.End.exists_eigenvalue over the algebraically closed field Qlb gives an eigenvalue alpha. It is nonzero because Frobenius is invertible. Let S be its eigenspace. Frobenius acts on S by alpha; multiplication by alpha inverse shows F(S)=S. Equip S and V/S with the restriction and quotient automorphisms. Their inclusion and projection are equivariant and form a short exact sequence. Since S is nonzero, the quotient has strictly smaller dimension. Every quotient eigenvalue is an eigenvalue of V by the already proved FrobeniusModule.hasEigenvalue_of_surjective in WeilConjectures.ZetaLinearAlgebra.FrobeniusModule.Map. Thus the induction hypothesis makes V/S mixed of weights at most w.

Write q=p^a>1 and t=2 log(norm(iota alpha))/log q. Nonvanishing of alpha gives positive norm. The real exponential/logarithm identities give q^(t/2)=norm(iota alpha); strict monotonicity of rpow in the exponent for q>1 and the assumed bound give t<=w. Every eigenvalue beta of the restriction to S equals alpha: apply the scalar-action identity to a nonzero beta-eigenvector and cancel the vector. Therefore S is pure of weight t, hence mixed by the two-term filtration from step 1. Apply lem-a1-extension-bounds to S -> V -> V/S to finish the induction.

proof_origin.place: Proof: eigenspace and quotient dimension induction replaces Jordan-Holder filtration; extension assembly uses lem-a1-extension-bounds
